questions.question: Which of the following functions is negligible in n?
questions.explanation: 2^{-n} is negligible: for any polynomial p, eventually 2^n > p(n), so 2^{-n} < 1/p(n). The others are all non-negligible: 1/n^{100} is an inverse polynomial (p(n)=n^{100} witnesses it), 1/n is 1/poly, and 0.0001 is a positive constant.

questions.question: A reduction proves: if adversary A breaks scheme X with advantage ε, then B breaks primitive Y with advantage ε/q(n) where q is polynomial. Why does this establish security of X?
options: If Y is hard, ε/q(n) must be negligible, so ε = q(n)·(ε/q(n)) is also negligible
Because q(n) is large, ε/q(n) is always negligible regardless of ε
Because B runs in exponential time, its advantage does not matter
The reduction proves X and Y have the same security level
questions.explanation: Hardness of Y means Adv_B = ε/q(n) is negligible. Since q is polynomial and ε/q is negligible, ε = q·(ε/q) = poly·negl = negl. So A cannot have non-negligible advantage against X.

questions.question: A scheme uses a 128-bit primitive. The security reduction has total loss factor 2^{20}. What is the concrete security of the scheme?
options: 108 bits
128 bits
148 bits
20 bits

questions.question: You want 128-bit scheme security. Your reduction chain has total loss 2^{30}. What primitive security level do you need?
options: 158 bits
128 bits
98 bits
30 bits

questions.question: Three reductions compose with loss factors 4, 8, and 16. What is the total loss?
questions.explanation: Total loss = product of per-hop losses = 4 × 8 × 16 = 512. Security bits eaten = log2(512) = 9.

questions.question: Is f(n) = 1/n^{100} negligible?
options: No — the polynomial p(n) = n^{100} witnesses f(n) ≥ 1/p(n) for all n
Yes — it is astronomically small at practical n
Yes — any inverse polynomial is negligible
It depends on the security parameter
questions.explanation: Negligible means below EVERY inverse polynomial. For p(n) = n^{100}, f(n) = 1/n^{100} = 1/p(n), which does not satisfy f(n) < 1/p(n). So f is non-negligible — it is exactly one particular inverse polynomial.

questions.question: Which operations preserve negligibility?
options: Multiplying a negligible function by a polynomial
Dividing one negligible function by another
Taking the reciprocal of a negligible function
Raising a negligible function to a negative exponent
questions.explanation: poly(n) × negl(n) = negl(n): for any polynomial p, choose q = poly·p; negl < 1/q = 1/(poly·p), so poly·negl < 1/p. Dividing or taking reciprocals of negligible functions can yield non-negligible (or even growing) functions.

questions.question: An adversary has advantage 2^{-64} against a scheme. Is this sufficient for 128-bit security?
options: No — 128-bit security requires advantage < 2^{-128}
Yes — 2^{-64} is negligible
Yes — 64 bits is half of 128, which is acceptable
It depends on the reduction loss factor
questions.explanation: 128-bit security means the adversary's advantage is at most 2^{-128}. An advantage of 2^{-64} gives only 64 security bits — half the target. The scheme is not 128-bit secure.
